props.title: Hobgoblins
props.initialSlug: Cheap puppets wreak havoc on unsuspecting teens

sections.content: Hobgoblins (1988) stands as one of the most notoriously inept low-budget horror comedies ever made, deliberately aping the success of Gremlins (1984) but failing spectacularly in execution. Director Rick Sloane created what became an instant "so-bad-it's-good" classic, featuring rubber puppet monsters that look like they were purchased at a discount Halloween store. The film gained legendary status after being featured on Mystery Science Theater 3000 (1988-1999), where it was mercilessly - and deservedly - ripped apart for its terrible effects, nonsensical plot, and wooden acting.

sections.content: The late 1980s saw a flood of low-budget creature features trying to capitalize on Gremlins (1984) success. Films like Critters (1986) and Ghoulies (1985) at least maintained some production standards, but Hobgoblins represented the bottom of the barrel. The film's plot about alien puppets that make people's fantasies come true - usually leading to death - borrows heavily from better movies while adding unintentionally hilarious dialogue and bizarre character choices.

The film's legacy lives on primarily through its MST3K appearance and as a touchstone for discussions of "best worst movies" alongside films like Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) and The Room (2003). The puppet effects are particularly noteworthy for their complete lack of believability - the hobgoblins appear to be simply thrown at actors by off-screen crew members. SUBHEAD: The Rise of "So Bad It's Good" Cinema

sections.content: While Hobgoblins helped establish the template for enjoyably terrible cinema, it arrived during a particularly fertile period for bad movies gaining cult status. Films like Miami Connection (1987) and Hard Ticket to Hawaii (1987) demonstrated how earnest incompetence could create unintentional entertainment value that audiences would celebrate decades later.
